name: Kalaripayattu training & demonstrations (Kalari schools)
tagline: Live demonstrations, short workshops and multi‑day kalari stays for travellers
summary: Kerala's kalari schools offer demonstrations, 1–3 hour workshops, drop‑in classes and residential short‑courses so travellers can watch, try or immerse in Kalaripayattu.
description: Kalaripayattu schools (kalaris) in Kerala teach and demonstrate one of India’s oldest martial arts. They open their kuzhi (sunken) arenas and halls to visitors for live demonstrations, short workshops and day or residential training.

Visitors get everything from staged performances to guided 1–3 hour introductory sessions, drop‑in practice classes and longer residential courses (days to weeks). Centres also link the art to Kalari Chikitsa (marma therapy), yoga and self‑defence programmes.

These kalari experiences connect travellers with living heritage: disciplined movement, weapon work, rhythm, guru–shishya etiquette and local storytelling traditions. Many respected schools welcome international students by prior arrangement; confirm schedules before you travel.
highlights: Short demonstrations and staged performances for visitors
1–3 hour introductory workshops and drop‑in classes
Residential short‑courses (14‑ to 30‑day style programmes) for deeper immersion
Kalari Chikitsa (marma/therapeutic) and self‑defence sessions in some centres
Authentic kuzhi kalari and guru‑led training in traditional settings

sections.heading: Background
body: Kalaripayattu is Kerala’s traditional martial art; training historically happens in a kalari (training arena). Modern kalari schools preserve movement sequences, weapon practice and therapeutic knowledge while presenting curated demonstrations for the public.

State tourism listings and established sanghams (like CVN) and independent gurukuls document a mixture of public performances, short visitor workshops and residential teacher‑training pathways. Communities regard demonstrations as both cultural display and a way to attract learners.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Watch a kuzhi‑kalari demonstration to see coordinated striking, sword and shield, long‑staff and flexible urumi work; performances often include rhythmic footwork, leaps and marma (vital‑point) demonstrations.

Try an introductory workshop or drop‑in class (many schools offer single‑session classes) to learn basics: body conditioning, the Ashta Vadivu postures, simple footwork and safe, supervised weapon handling drills.

For deeper practice, book a short residential programme (commonly 2–14 days or longer) to join morning and evening sessions, communal meals and a taste of gurukulam life. Some centres pair training with marma therapy, yoga and cultural tours.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Decide what you want: a short demo, a 1–3 hour workshop, a drop‑in class, or a residential stay. Contact the kalari in advance for availability, language support and any medical/fitness restrictions. Many want prior notice for workshops or residential admissions.

Major kalari hubs include Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode, Alappuzha, Ernakulam and Wayanad; reach them via the nearest airport or train and take a taxi to the school. Confirm exact address, timings and any fees with the school before travelling.

latest.text: Kalari Kendram lists upcoming residential batch start dates (7 Nov 2026) and continues to promote drop‑in classes and short residential programmes for travellers and international students.
Kerala Tourism highlights multiple kalari centres (Agasthyam, CVN branches, Ekaveera and others) as places where visitors can attend demonstrations or arrange short‑term training sessions.

Agasthyam Kalari (Thiruvananthapuram) advertises residential 14‑day and 30‑day foundation programmes and says workshops and demonstrations are available to international visitors by prior arrangement.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Year‑round; post‑monsoon and tourist season (Oct–Mar) are easiest for travel and outdoor components.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Major kalari centres sit near Trivandrum, Kozhikode, Kochi, Alappuzha and Thrissur. Fly to the nearest airport (Trivandrum/Calicut/Cochin) or use mainline trains, then take a taxi to the kalari; confirm directions and pickup with the school.
etiquette: Book workshops or residential stays in advance and confirm start times — many schools need prior notice.
Wear comfortable, flexible clothes and be ready to train barefoot; disclose injuries or health issues before physical sessions.
Respect guru–shishya etiquette: follow instructor instructions, ask before photographing, and remove footwear at the kalari entrance.
Ask about insurance, cancellation and safety measures for weapon work; beginner sessions always use adapted or wooden weapons.
